notes: Friday 13 Nov 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Thu 12 Nov. Economy: 10-year Treasury yield back above 5%; US home sales 16-year low; UK GDP +0.7% on AI; Family Dollar $63m overcharging settlement. Tech: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO; Microsoft 365 outage; Cerebras +17% with Microsoft deal; public-sector unions win AI protections. Politics: Putin hard line with US envoys; Holscher wins Kansas governor; Trump says no Iran deal needed; new socialist mayors. Literature (US): Jane Schoenbrun's debut novel; Ben Lerner's Transcription audiobook; Lit Hub's 10 overlooked debuts; Gopnik on The Sun Also Rises at 100. Society: Afghan women and male-doctor ban; US measles deaths; Brooklyn building collapse; Ebola aid money missing in DR Congo.

stories.headline: US 10-year Treasury yield jumps back above 5% as oil climbs and more Fed hikes are expected
stories.dek: Trump's 'we don't need a deal with Iran' pushed oil up. Traders now see a December rate hike as certain.
stories.caveman: When the US government borrows money, it sells IOUs called Treasury bonds. The 'yield' is the interest it must pay. On Thursday the 10-year yield rose to about 5.13%, back above 5%. That number matters because mortgages, car loans and credit cards follow it. Two things pushed it up. First, oil: after President Trump said 'We don't need a deal with Iran,' people feared the Middle East war would drag on, and US oil rose over 2% to about $88.74 a barrel while Brent hit about $95.82. Second, inflation: a hot price report earlier this week made traders expect the Federal Reserve to keep raising rates. Markets now price a 100% chance of a December hike, and Goldman Sachs added another hike for March.
stories.why_it_matters: Higher yields mean more expensive borrowing for families and companies everywhere, and they often pull money out of riskier markets, including Taiwan stocks.
stories.camps: Fed hawks say higher rates are needed to beat inflation. Critics say the hikes are crushing housing and that tariffs and the Iran war, not too much spending, are driving prices up.
stories.image_alt: Traders at work on a stock exchange floor

terms.explain: The interest rate the US government pays when it borrows by selling bonds.
One-hundredth of a percentage point (0.01%).
A main global oil price benchmark.
When the central bank raises interest rates to cool prices.

stories.headline: US home sales fall to a 16-year low as mortgage rates near 7.2%
stories.dek: Only 3.75 million existing homes sold in October, down 8.8% from last year. Typical price: $416,700.
stories.caveman: Buying a home in the US usually means taking a big loan called a mortgage. In early 2026 the usual 30-year mortgage rate dipped below 6%. Now, with inflation and the Iran war pushing rates up, it is about 7.18%. That makes monthly payments much bigger, so fewer people buy. The National Association of Realtors said sales of already-built homes fell to a yearly pace of 3.75 million in October, the lowest since August 2010. Yet prices did not fall: the middle price rose a little to $416,700, because few owners want to sell and give up their old cheap loans. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023 and is expected to raise again in December.
stories.why_it_matters: Housing is the biggest cost for most families. Frozen home sales also hurt jobs in building, furniture and moving, and show how rate hikes hit ordinary people.
stories.camps: Some economists say the pain is the price of beating inflation. Housing advocates say the real fix is building far more homes and that high rates mostly lock young and lower-income buyers out.
stories.image_alt: A residential subdivision in Queen Creek, Arizona
stories.image_credit: Photo: David Blakeman for The Washington Post via Getty Images

terms.explain: A loan used to buy a home, paid back monthly over many years.
Sales of homes that were already built, not brand-new ones.
The middle price: half of homes sold for more, half for less.
Owners stay put because selling would mean giving up a cheap old loan.

stories.headline: AI helps the UK economy grow 0.7%, its fastest pace in two and a half years
stories.dek: IT and computer services led the July–September growth. Chancellor John Healey called it 'standout resilience.'
stories.caveman: GDP is the total value of everything a country makes and sells. Britain's statistics office said GDP grew 0.7% from July to September, the best quarter since early 2024. Almost all of it came from services, led by information and communication, which grew 2.1%. Companies selling AI and cloud computing reported the biggest jumps in sales, and back-office work like admin also grew as firms used more AI. Chancellor (finance minister) John Healey said the UK is growing at its fastest rate in almost 10 years, outside the Covid period. September alone grew 0.2%, but August was revised down to zero.
stories.why_it_matters: It is one of the first clear signs that AI spending is showing up in a big economy's numbers, not just in tech stock prices.
stories.camps: Optimists say AI is a new engine for growth. Skeptics warn the boost may fade, that high oil prices from the Iran war still threaten households, and that AI gains may go to companies more than workers.
stories.image_alt: People walking along the Thames with the City of London skyline behind

terms.explain: Gross domestic product: the total value of goods and services an economy produces.
A three-month period of the year.
Office for National Statistics, the UK government data agency.
Businesses that sell work, not physical goods: IT, banks, shops, admin.

stories.headline: Family Dollar to pay $63m over charging more at the register than on the shelf
stories.dek: The FTC and 17 states acted after a Guardian investigation found the chain failed 2,100+ price checks.
stories.caveman: Family Dollar is a US discount store chain with about 7,000 shops, often in poorer towns. Government inspectors kept finding that the price on the shelf was lower than what customers paid at checkout, for things like milk, diapers, batteries and toilet paper. A Guardian investigation found Family Dollar failed at least 2,100 price inspections in 20 states from 2022 to late 2025. On Thursday the Federal Trade Commission and 17 states announced a $63m settlement. Their lawsuit says the company knew it was hurting customers and still overcharges. Family Dollar did not admit or deny the claims and says it takes pricing accuracy seriously.
stories.why_it_matters: Small overcharges add up for families on tight budgets, who shop at dollar stores the most. It also shows how reporting can lead to enforcement.
stories.camps: Consumer groups say $63m is small for a chain this big and want stronger checks. The company says it is improving. Some argue regulators should also look at rival Dollar General, which had similar problems.
stories.image_alt: A Family Dollar store in Windsor, North Carolina

terms.explain: An agreement to end a legal case, often by paying money, without a trial.
Federal Trade Commission: the US agency that protects consumers from unfair business.
A government check that shelf prices match checkout prices.
A cheap store selling basic goods at low prices.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after affair scandals; CFO Colette Kress steps in
stories.dek: Shares fell 13% at the open and closed down 4.3%, wiping about $180bn in a day. Trump says Tim Cook should take over.
stories.caveman: Nvidia makes the chips that power most of the world's AI. Its co-founder Jensen Huang, born in Taiwan, ran it for over 30 years. In recent days reports said he had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a Nvidia customer whom US authorities link to Chinese intelligence, and later with two company employees. On Thursday he quit as CEO, president and board member, effective immediately. Finance chief Colette Kress is interim CEO while the board searches inside and outside the company. The board's statement praised his 'profound' contributions and did not mention the scandal. A top law firm is investigating. President Trump posted that only Apple's Tim Cook could replace him.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is worth about $4 trillion and buys huge amounts from Taiwan firms like TSMC and Foxconn. The scandal also feeds a push in Washington for tighter chip limits on China.
stories.camps: Some say resigning protects the company and that Nvidia is bigger than one man. Others warn it loses its key visionary. Critics on the left say the saga shows tech bosses hold too much unchecked power over markets and politics.
stories.image_alt: Jensen Huang, who has resigned as chief executive of Nvidia

terms.explain: Chief executive officer: the top boss running a company.
Temporary, until a permanent choice is made.
A group that oversees a company for its shareholders and can hire or fire the CEO.
What all of a company’s shares are worth together.

stories.headline: Widespread Microsoft outage knocks out Outlook, Teams and other 365 services
stories.dek: About 130,000 people reported Outlook problems at the peak. Microsoft blamed servers going down and straining the rest.
stories.caveman: On Thursday afternoon (US Eastern time) many people around the world could not use Microsoft's Outlook email, Teams chat or other Microsoft 365 tools. Outage tracker Downdetector showed about 130,000 reports for Outlook alone. Microsoft first said there was 'elevated load', meaning too much traffic. Later it said some servers unexpectedly went offline, which put too much pressure on the rest, and some servers were failing automatic health checks. Engineers used a different way to check server health and began bringing machines back. Some users also reported Amazon and Google problems, but Amazon said its services were working normally.
stories.why_it_matters: Huge numbers of schools, offices and governments run on a few cloud companies. When one stumbles, work stops in many places at once.
stories.camps: Microsoft says it is fixing the cause and adding automatic recovery. Critics say relying on a handful of giant providers is risky and businesses should have backup plans.
stories.image_alt: Microsoft sign outside a company office (Reuters photo used by CNBC)

terms.explain: When a service stops working for users.
Microsoft’s online bundle of Outlook, Word, Excel, Teams and more.
A powerful computer that runs services for many users over the internet.
Computing services run in big remote data centers instead of on your own device.

stories.headline: AI chipmaker Cerebras jumps 17% after strong results and a new Microsoft deal
stories.dek: The Nvidia rival expects revenue to triple in 2027. Its stock had lost about 47% since its May debut.
stories.caveman: Cerebras makes giant AI chips that try to compete with Nvidia's graphics processors (GPUs). On Thursday it reported better sales than experts expected, with core revenue up 70%, and said it signed a deal with Microsoft in October that should start bringing money in early 2027. It already has deals with Amazon and Oracle. CEO Andrew Feldman said long waits and high prices for GPUs create an opening for Cerebras. It expects $310m to $330m in revenue next quarter and roughly triple revenue in 2027. Shares rose 17% after hours. The news came the same day Nvidia's CEO resigned.
stories.why_it_matters: If AI customers can buy from more chip companies, Nvidia's grip loosens. That could change who orders chips from Taiwan's factories.
stories.camps: Fans say Cerebras proves Nvidia can be challenged. Skeptics note the stock had nearly halved since its listing and the company still needs money to keep up with demand.
stories.image_alt: A speaker on stage at a tech conference (Getty photo used by CNBC for the Cerebras story)

terms.explain: Graphics processing unit: a chip that does many calculations at once, now key for AI.
A company’s regular update on how much it sold and earned.
What a company says it expects to earn in the future.
Stock trading after the main market closes.

stories.headline: US public workers are fighting to protect their jobs from AI — and some are winning
stories.dek: Oakland city workers voted 94% to authorize a strike and won a deal: retrain or reassign workers replaced by AI, don't fire them.
stories.caveman: Public workers are people employed by governments: city clerks, subway inspectors, data staff. In Oakland, California, the union IFPTE Local 21 worried the city would bring in AI that watches workers and judges them unfairly, or replaces them. On 22 October members voted 94.1% to allow a strike. The city then agreed to a three-year tentative deal with AI protections, including retraining or moving workers whose jobs AI takes instead of firing them, so the strike was put on hold. Unions across the US, including New York transit workers, are seeking similar rules. Transport Workers Union president John Samuelsen said members see automation as 'the ultimate threat to their jobs.'
stories.why_it_matters: This is a test of whether workers get a say in how AI is used at work. Deals in big cities can become models elsewhere, including in Asia.
stories.camps: Unions say AI is often sold as a 'fancy new toy' that costs more and works worse, and that people need protection. Some officials say AI can save taxpayer money and rules should not block useful tools.
stories.image_alt: IFPTE union members rally in Oakland, California

terms.explain: A group of workers who join together to bargain with their employer.
A vote that allows union leaders to call a strike if talks fail.
A deal reached by negotiators that still needs final approval.
Using machines or software to do work people used to do.

stories.headline: Putin takes a hard line in talks with US envoys as Ukraine reports new Starlink disruptions
stories.dek: Putin demanded all four Ukrainian regions Russia claims and said any foreign troops in Ukraine would be targets. Europe will join the next round.
stories.caveman: Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin on Thursday to push a peace deal. Putin refused to give ground: he wants full control of four Ukrainian regions Russia says it annexed, and he said foreign peacekeeping troops in Ukraine would be treated as 'continuation of war' and targeted. That cooled hopes raised by Ukraine's President Zelenskyy, who saw a 'window' for a deal before the end of 2026. Witkoff said European representatives will join the next talks. The envoys then flew to Dublin to brief Zelenskyy. Meanwhile, Ukraine's military reported new problems with Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet, which its troops rely on.
stories.why_it_matters: How this war ends shapes how big powers treat smaller neighbors, which matters to Taiwan too.
stories.camps: Some argue any ceasefire is better than more deaths. Ukraine and many Europeans say giving Russia land rewards invasion and invites future attacks. Others question relying on a private company's satellites in war.
stories.image_alt: Vladimir Putin meeting US envoys at the Kremlin

terms.explain: A person sent by a government to negotiate for it.
To take over another country’s land and claim it as your own.
Foreign troops sent to help keep a ceasefire.
SpaceX’s satellite internet service, owned by Elon Musk.

stories.headline: Democrat Cindy Holscher wins Kansas governor race, holding a seat Republicans hoped to flip
stories.dek: She beat Trump-endorsed Ty Masterson in a red state, running on public schools and against 'sweetheart deals' for billionaires.
stories.caveman: Kansas usually votes Republican for president, but it has had a Democratic governor, Laura Kelly, for eight years. She could not run again, so this was seen as the governor's race most likely to flip to Republicans out of 36 this year. The Associated Press called it for Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher, 57, over Republican Senate President Ty Masterson, whom Trump endorsed. Holscher opposed school vouchers and wanted more money for public schools, called for a pause on new data centers, and backed legal cannabis to raise state money. She tied Masterson to an old Republican tax cut that caused budget crises. Masterson promised lower property taxes and called her 'the most radical, liberal, socialist Democrat ever.'
stories.why_it_matters: It adds to a strong Democratic midterm, and shows populist economic messages can win even in conservative places.
stories.camps: Democrats see proof that kitchen-table issues beat culture-war labels. Republicans say Kansas has a long habit of picking Democratic governors to balance a Republican legislature, so it says little nationally.
stories.image_alt: Cindy Holscher speaks to reporters after voting early in Kansas City, Kansas

terms.explain: When a seat changes from one party to the other.
Public money given to families to pay for private schools.
To publicly support a candidate.
When a news group like AP declares a winner based on vote counts.

stories.headline: Trump says the US doesn't need a deal to end the Iran war and tells Vance to focus on 'Democrat-run cities'
stories.dek: Vance had been talking with go-betweens in Iran and Qatar about new talks. The move locks in a tense stalemate.
stories.caveman: The US and Israel started striking Iran in February. Iran answered by closing the Strait of Hormuz, a key sea lane for oil, and fuel prices jumped worldwide. The US now blockades Iranian ports and has mostly reopened the strait, but there has been no big fighting for months. Vice President JD Vance had reportedly been talking with intermediaries about restarting peace talks. On Thursday Trump posted, 'We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,' and told Vance to put his attention on what Trump called 'Massive Corruption and Crime' in Democrat-run cities and states.
stories.why_it_matters: No deal means the risk of higher oil prices stays, which affects gas, electricity and shipping costs in Taiwan and everywhere.
stories.camps: Supporters say the US already has the upper hand and does not need to give Iran anything. Critics say a frozen war keeps oil high and danger alive, and that sending Vance after Democratic cities is political, not about safety.
stories.image_alt: Donald Trump and JD Vance at a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery

terms.explain: A narrow sea passage near Iran that much of the world’s oil passes through.
Using ships or force to stop goods going in or out of ports.
A situation where neither side wins and nothing moves.
A go-between who passes messages between two sides.

stories.headline: A new wave of socialist mayors is coming — from Los Angeles to Washington DC. Can they deliver?
stories.dek: DSA members Nithya Raman (LA) and Janeese Lewis George (DC) won, joining NYC's Zohran Mamdani. DSA's seats in Congress will quadruple to eight.
stories.caveman: The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) is a left-wing group inside US politics that pushes for cheaper housing, public services and workers' rights. In last week's elections its members won big. Nithya Raman will lead Los Angeles, the second-biggest US city, and Janeese Lewis George will lead Washington DC. Young members David Morales and Yousef Rabhi won mayor races in Providence and Ann Arbor. They join New York's mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose long-shot win is credited with inspiring the wave. From January, DSA will have eight members in Congress and over 100 endorsed officials nationwide. But mayors run practical things like garbage pickup and snow days, so they must prove their ideas work. Mamdani said: 'If politics cannot deliver on the block where you live, why would you trust it to deliver anywhere?'
stories.why_it_matters: City leaders shape rent, transit and policing. These mayors will be a real-world test of left-wing ideas on affordability.
stories.camps: Supporters say voters want bold help with living costs. Critics, including moderate Democrats, worry about taxes, business flight and promises that are hard to pay for. Even fans admit the stakes are high: failures would hurt the movement.

terms.explain: Democratic Socialists of America, a left-wing political organization.
A person who has won a mayor election but has not taken office yet.
Whether ordinary people can pay for basics like rent and food.
To officially back a candidate.

stories.headline: Who's hot: filmmaker Jane Schoenbrun's first novel turns screen-culture horror into a book
stories.dek: The 'I Saw the TV Glow' director's Public Access Afterworld follows a trans content moderator chasing a cult leader through TV static.
stories.caveman: Jane Schoenbrun is an American filmmaker known for the cult horror movie I Saw the TV Glow, about people pulled into the world behind a screen. Now they have written a first novel, Public Access Afterworld. The hero, Bethany Peters, is a young trans woman whose job is to watch disturbing videos and delete the ones that break the rules at a YouTube-like company. One night she sees a video by a non-binary kid who hurts themself for a mysterious figure called David Sawyer, and she sets off to save them. The book jumps between a youth psych ward, a lonely teen seeing images in TV static, and Los Alamos during the atomic bomb project. The Guardian review calls Schoenbrun 'wonderfully brutal, passionate and astute' about how the internet feeds on its victims. (Content note: self-harm.)
stories.why_it_matters: Moving between film and books, Schoenbrun is one of the most talked-about trans voices in American culture right now.
stories.camps: Fans praise the book's sharp take on online life. Some readers may find its many strands and dark themes hard going.
stories.image_credit: Photo: Monica Schipper/Getty Images for IMDb

terms.explain: A worker who reviews posts and videos and removes ones that break the rules.
A person who does not identify only as a man or a woman.
A movie with a small but very devoted fan base.
An author’s first published novel.

stories.headline: Ben Lerner's 'Transcription' arrives as an audiobook: a writer loses his phone and has to remember
stories.dek: The narrator drops his iPhone in a sink before interviewing his 90-year-old mentor, so he fakes recording and memorizes instead.
stories.caveman: Ben Lerner is a leading American novelist and poet. His short novel Transcription starts on a train to Providence, Rhode Island. The unnamed narrator is going to interview his old mentor Thomas, a famous German writer and film-maker who is 90. At the hotel he drops his iPhone in a sink and kills it. Now he cannot record the talk or video-call his young daughter at bedtime. He pretends to record on the dead phone and tries to keep Thomas's words in his memory. The book thinks about memory, storytelling and how phones shape our lives. The Guardian says actor Seth Numrich reads the audiobook well, handling Lerner's layered writing.
stories.why_it_matters: Lerner is a big name in literary fiction, and this book captures something everyone feels: panic and freedom without a phone.
stories.camps: Admirers love his clever, thoughtful style. Others find his self-aware narrators too inward-looking for their taste.

terms.explain: A story longer than a short story but shorter than a novel.
A book read aloud and recorded for listening.
The voice telling the story.
The invisible line between a story and its audience; breaking it means speaking to the reader directly.

stories.headline: Lit Hub picks 10 great debut novels you might have missed in 2026
stories.dek: First books by Emeline Atwood, Bindu Bansinath, Mary H.K. Choi, T Kira Madden, Larissa Pham and others get a boost.
stories.caveman: A debut novel is a writer's first. Lit Hub says it has become harder than ever for new fiction writers without a track record to get attention, so it listed favorites (not 'the best'). They include Emeline Atwood's A Real Animal, about a young woman's ordinary days until something terrible happens; Bindu Bansinath's Men Like Ours, where women in an Indian-American New Jersey suburb gossip in a WhatsApp group until it becomes a murder mystery; Mary H.K. Choi's Pool House, called the novel of the summer, about a messy mother-daughter bond; plus T Kira Madden's Whidbey, Larissa Pham's Discipline, Bobuq Sayed's No God But Us, Avigayl Sharp's Offseason and Nafissa Thompson-Spires's The Four Wives and Five Deaths of Richard Milford.
stories.why_it_matters: Lists like this help new authors, many of them women and writers of color, get noticed beyond one or two hyped books a year.
stories.camps: Readers welcome the spotlight. Some note that one person's list reflects personal taste, and the publishing industry still pours money into a few big titles.

terms.explain: A first work, like a writer’s first novel.
A history of past success.
Fiction focused on character, ideas and style more than plot formulas.
Literary Hub, a US website about books and writing.

stories.headline: Still hot at 100: Adam Gopnik on why Hemingway's 'The Sun Also Rises' lives on
stories.dek: The 1926 Lost Generation novel has dated prejudices, but its plain, 'go somewhere, do a thing' style still shapes American fiction.
stories.caveman: Ernest Hemingway's The Sun Also Rises came out in 1926. It follows American and British expats drinking in Paris and going to bullfights in Spain after World War I. Writer Adam Gopnik admits new readers will hit ugly parts: anti-Jewish jabs at the character Robert Cohn, slights about gay men, and a heroine judged for her desires. A Reddit reader even called it 'a boring travel vlog… people going to a place and doing a thing.' Gopnik says that is almost exactly right, and that is the genius: Hemingway stripped writing of heavy symbols and sermons and told the details of going places and doing things. That clear style became a model for much American fiction after it.
stories.why_it_matters: Classics turning 100 make us ask what to keep and what to criticize. This is a good guide to reading old books with open eyes.
stories.camps: Fans call it the purest American prose style. Critics say its bigotry and macho world should not be brushed aside, and that other writers of the time deserve as much attention.
stories.image_alt: Repeated illustration in the style of The Sun Also Rises' classic cover art (Lit Hub lead image)

terms.explain: The young people who came of age during World War I, many of them writers living in Paris.
Someone living outside their home country.
Hatred of or prejudice against Jewish people.
Ordinary written language, not poetry.

stories.headline: Afghan women told to 'go home' as a de facto ban on male doctors treating them spreads
stories.dek: No public law was announced, but the Taliban's vice ministry has ordered male dentists not to treat women, and raids enforce it.
stories.caveman: In Afghanistan, the Taliban already bar most women from school and many jobs, so there are few female doctors. Now women say male doctors are refusing them. Farida, 37, in Herat, paid in advance for dental work, but at her third visit the clinic told her to go home: an order from the Ministry for the Propagation of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice said male dentists could no longer treat women. Three months later her treatment is still unfinished and she can barely eat. The Guardian and Zan Times found the rule appears to have spread across the country without a public announcement, with security forces raiding clinics and warning male doctors. Male doctors have also been told not to examine women without a male guardian present.
stories.why_it_matters: If women can't see male doctors and can't train to become doctors, many simply cannot get health care. It is a clear case of gender rules putting lives at risk.
stories.camps: The Taliban present their rules as religious and cultural. Women's rights groups, the UN and doctors call it gender apartheid and say it is causing preventable suffering and death.
stories.image_alt: Doctors at a hospital in Afghanistan

terms.explain: True in practice, even if not written into law.
The hardline Islamist group that has ruled Afghanistan since 2021.
In Islamic tradition, a close male relative who can accompany a woman.
A system that separates and oppresses people based on gender.

stories.headline: US reports six measles deaths in 2026 as it faces its worst outbreak in 35 years
stories.dek: More than 5,400 cases nationwide. A senator is investigating whether health secretary RFK Jr misled Congress.
stories.caveman: Measles is a very contagious virus that can kill, especially young kids. A vaccine prevents it, and the US declared measles eliminated in 2000. Now, with fewer kids vaccinated, it is back. The CDC listed six measles-related deaths this year, twice last year's number, and more than 5,400 cases, the most since 1991. Pennsylvania was hit hardest. A child died in New York on election day and an infant died in Wisconsin days later. The CDC changed how it counts deaths after reports that health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, a longtime vaccine skeptic, asked it not to count two Pennsylvania deaths; he had claimed without evidence they might not be measles. A senator has opened an investigation into whether Kennedy lied to Congress.
stories.why_it_matters: Outbreaks anywhere can spread through travel. It also shows how trust in vaccines and in health agencies affects real lives.
stories.camps: Public health experts say vaccines are safe and the government is weakening protection. Kennedy and his supporters say they want more 'choice' and questions about vaccines; critics say that message is costing children's lives.
stories.image_alt: Medical providers assess a patient with measles symptoms in South Carolina
stories.image_credit: Photo: Juan Diego Reyes for The Washington Post via Getty Images

terms.explain: A highly contagious virus causing fever and rash; can be deadly.
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the US public health agency.
No longer spreading inside the country year-round.
A sudden rise in cases of a disease in one area.

stories.headline: Brooklyn building collapse kills eight, including two children; 18 hurt
stories.dek: The three-storey home next to a construction site in Flatbush fell. Mayor Mamdani says he is 'heartbroken'; rescuers keep searching in the rain.
stories.caveman: On Wednesday at about 4pm, a three-storey residential building on the edge of a construction site on Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn, New York, suddenly fell down. Six people were found dead in the rubble and two more died later, eight in total. Two were children, and two were construction workers from the nearby site. At least 18 people were hurt, including four firefighters. About 250 firefighters and rescuers kept digging through 'extremely dangerous conditions,' said Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who urged people to stay away. Fire commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said they were still in rescue mode and would assume more people could be trapped until they search under the heavy debris.
stories.why_it_matters: It raises hard questions about construction safety next to homes, and about who checks old buildings in a crowded city.
stories.camps: Officials are focused on rescue first. Tenant and worker groups want answers on whether the construction work weakened the building and whether warnings were ignored.
stories.image_alt: Firefighters rescue a person after the Brooklyn building collapse

terms.explain: Broken pieces of a fallen building.
Firefighters, police and medics who arrive first at emergencies.
A neighborhood in Brooklyn, New York City.
Rescue means looking for living people; recovery means retrieving bodies.

stories.headline: Ebola in DR Congo: millions in aid money go missing while health workers go unpaid, MSF warns
stories.dek: More than 5,400 have died since May, the second-deadliest Ebola outbreak ever. Some ambulances ran out of fuel.
stories.caveman: Ebola is a deadly virus spread through contact with body fluids. An outbreak declared in May in the Democratic Republic of Congo has infected 11,000 people and killed more than 5,400. The medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF, Doctors Without Borders) says the outbreak is 'out of control,' yet front-line workers are going unpaid, lack training and are short of basic supplies; some ambulances have run out of fuel. Hundreds of millions of dollars meant for the response are not reaching the people who need it. Last month, Africa CDC said $700m out of $962m sent to groups running the response was unaccounted for. MSF wants the government and UN agencies to track money better and send it where needs are greatest.
stories.why_it_matters: When aid money disappears, disease spreads further and donors lose trust, which makes the next emergency harder for everyone.
stories.camps: Aid groups demand accountability. The Congolese government has been asked for comment. Some experts also point to aid cuts by rich countries that left the system weaker in the first place.
stories.image_alt: Ebola response workers in DR Congo

terms.explain: A severe, often deadly virus spread by contact with an infected person’s body fluids.
Médecins Sans Frontières, or Doctors Without Borders, an international medical charity.
Missing, with no record of where it went.
The African Union’s public health agency.
